title: Living with Gravity & Friction
subtitle: The other forces that act while gravity pulls.
objectives: Explain the normal force and why you do not fall through the floor
Explain buoyancy and what decides whether something floats
Describe tension and thrust as forces in a direction
Identify which forces are acting in a given everyday situation

cards.title: Gravity pulls you down. Why are you not moving?
cards.text: Because something is pushing back, exactly as hard. Most of physics is finding the force that balances the one you noticed first.

cards.title: The floor pushes up on you
cards.text: Normal here means perpendicular — at right angles to the surface. It has nothing to do with ordinary.
points: **The floor bends slightly** under you, like a very stiff spring.
**It pushes back** exactly hard enough to stop you sinking.
**Push harder** and it pushes harder, until it breaks.
**Standing still** means the push up equals the pull down.

question.text: Why do you not sink through the floor?
options: Your weight becomes zero when standing
The floor pushes up with a normal force equal to your weight
question.explain: The floor deforms a little and pushes back perpendicular to its surface, exactly balancing your weight.

cards.title: Water pushes up on whatever is in it
cards.text: Put something in water and it displaces some. The water pushes back with the weight of what was moved aside.
points: **Displace more weight than you are** and you float.
**Displace less** and you sink.
**That is why a steel ship floats**: it is mostly air inside the hull.
**Crush the same steel into a block** and it sinks at once.

cards.title: Why floodwater lifts a car you could not push
cards.text: A car weighs over a tonne, and about thirty centimetres of moving water will shift it.
points: **Buoyancy takes most of its weight**, so the tyres barely grip.
**Less grip means less friction**, so the water only has to beat a little.
**Moving water pushes hard** — it is far denser than air.
**Never drive into flood water.** The maths is not on your side.

question.text: A steel ship floats because steel is lighter than water.
question.explain: Steel is far denser than water. The hull floats because it encloses enough air to displace more weight than the ship has.

cards.title: Pulls and pushes, named by direction
cards.text: Tension is a pull along something stretched. Thrust is a push that drives something forward.
points: **Tension** runs along a rope, cable or chain. Rope only pulls.
**Thrust** comes from an engine, a propeller or a leg.
**Both have a direction**, which is the whole point of naming them.
**A tow rope** is tension; the engine doing the towing is thrust.

cards.title: A race car wing pushes down, not up
cards.text: A plane's wing lifts. Turn the same shape upside down and it presses the car into the road instead.
points: **More downforce** means a bigger normal force on the tyres.
**Bigger normal force** means more grip, so faster cornering.
**It costs drag**, so straight-line speed suffers.
**At low speed it does nothing.** Downforce needs airflow.

cards.title: A fan makes thrust, and feels it
cards.text: Push air one way and the air pushes the fan the other way. That is why a loose fan creeps backwards.
points: **The blade throws air forward.** The air shoves the blade back.
**The stand is weighted** so that push does not tip it.
**A drone uses the same thrust** pointed downward to hold itself up.
**Every push has a push back.** Always.

question.text: Which force is a rope able to apply?
question.explain: A rope can pull but cannot push. That is tension, and it only works along the rope.

terms.def: The push a surface gives at right angles to itself.
The upward push of a fluid on whatever is in it.
The amount of fluid pushed aside by an object.
A pulling force along something stretched.
A pushing force that drives something forward.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Standing still means forces balance, not that none are acting.
Floating depends on displaced weight, not on the material alone.
Rope pulls, engines push. Tension and thrust.
Thirty centimetres of moving water can move a car.

quiz.text: What does 'normal' mean in normal force?
options: At right angles to the surface
quiz.explain: Normal is a geometry word here: perpendicular to the surface.
quiz.objective: Explain the normal force and why you do not fall through the floor

quiz.text: An object floats when it displaces…
options: more weight of fluid than its own
less weight of fluid than its own
quiz.explain: Displace more weight than you have and the upward push wins.
quiz.objective: Explain buoyancy and what decides whether something floats

quiz.text: Why does a steel ship float?
options: The hull encloses enough air to displace a lot of water
Steel is less dense than water
quiz.explain: Shape, not material. Crush the hull flat and the same steel sinks.
quiz.objective: Explain buoyancy and what decides whether something floats

quiz.text: A rope towing a car is under…
quiz.explain: Rope pulls along its length. It cannot push.
quiz.objective: Describe tension and thrust as forces in a direction

quiz.text: If you are standing still, no forces are acting on you.
quiz.explain: Two big ones are: gravity down and the normal force up. They balance.
quiz.objective: Identify which forces are acting in a given everyday situation

quiz.text: Why can thirty centimetres of moving water move a car?
options: Buoyancy removes much of its weight, so the tyres lose grip
quiz.explain: Less weight on the tyres means less friction, so the push of the water wins.
quiz.objective: Identify which forces are acting in a given everyday situation

quiz.text: A fan blowing forward feels a push backwards. Why?
options: Pushing air one way means the air pushes back the other way
quiz.explain: Every push has an equal push back, which is why the stand is weighted.
quiz.objective: Describe tension and thrust as forces in a direction

quiz.explain: A propeller drives something forward. Rope and chain can only pull.
quiz.objective: Describe tension and thrust as forces in a direction

quiz.text: The normal force is always equal to the object's weight.
quiz.explain: Only on level ground with nothing else pushing. On a slope, or if you press down, it differs.
quiz.objective: Explain the normal force and why you do not fall through the floor

quiz.text: The upward push of water on a submerged object is called…
quiz.explain: Buoyant force, equal to the weight of fluid displaced.
quiz.objective: Explain buoyancy and what decides whether something floats

quiz.text: A drone hovers by pointing thrust…
quiz.explain: Its rotors throw air downward, so the air pushes the drone up.
quiz.objective: Describe tension and thrust as forces in a direction

quiz.text: Which pair is balanced when a book rests on a table?
quiz.explain: Gravity pulls it down, the table pushes up, and nothing moves.
quiz.objective: Identify which forces are acting in a given everyday situation

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 6 Science, continuing the scope's gravity-and-friction strand into the other forces that act alongside them. The organising idea is that stillness means balance, not absence — stated once and then tested from three directions. Buoyancy is taught through displaced weight rather than 'light things float', which is the usual error, and the steel-ship case is used to break it. The flood card is deliberately practical: thirty centimetres of moving water is the figure worth him remembering.
discussion: If you are standing still, what is pushing up?
Why does shape decide whether steel floats?
Why is a fan stand heavy?
extension: Float a ball of foil, then crush it and float it again.
Push down on a bathroom scale and watch the normal force change.
misconceptions: That no forces act on something at rest.
That light materials float and heavy ones sink.
